slides.title: Understanding Generator Functions
slides.prompt: A generator function uses the 'yield' statement instead of 'return'. Calling a generator function returns a generator object without executing the body immediately. Values are produced lazily as requested.
slides.codeSnippet:
def count_up_to(max_num):
    count = 1
    while count <= max_num:
        yield count
        count += 1

counter = count_up_to(3)
print(next(counter))  # 1
print(next(counter))  # 2

slides.title: Generator Execution Behavior
slides.prompt: What happens when a generator function is invoked (e.g., `gen = my_generator()`)?
options: A generator object is created, but no function code is executed until next() is called
The entire function runs immediately and returns a list of values
It evaluates up to the first return statement
It starts a new background thread
slides.correctAnswer: A generator object is created, but no function code is executed until next() is called

slides.title: State Preservation in Generators
slides.prompt: What happens to a generator function's local variables when it hits a `yield` statement?
options: Local variables and execution state are frozen until the next call
Local variables are wiped and reset to None
Local variables are saved to global scope
The stack frame is destroyed permanently
slides.correctAnswer: Local variables and execution state are frozen until the next call

slides.title: Memory Efficiency of Generators
slides.prompt: Why are generators considered more memory efficient than lists for large datasets?
options: Generators compute values lazily one at a time on demand rather than storing everything in RAM
Generators store elements using compressed binary format
Generators automatically write overflow items to swap memory disk space
slides.correctAnswer: Generators compute values lazily one at a time on demand rather than storing everything in RAM
